indep.text: Seat indep present. Vantage: the author of a result must not be its checker; same-substrate agreement is coherence, not independent evidence.

plan.text: Seat plan present. I write and read draft plans, so I care about review that changes the draft: missing steps, wrong dependencies, unstated assumptions, and checks that would not catch a bad landing. Grading the prose is not the job. Independent eyes matter; the shape of the review matters more than the headcount.

cost.text: For routine plan checks, move that one independent reviewer from another model family be the default. It is the lowest-latency, lowest-token, lowest-steward-attention check and preserves the key independence property. Use a council only when the plan is high-risk, unusually ambiguous, or the first review exposes disagreement: its extra seats and coordination cost are justified only when they are likely to change the action.

fam.text: Recommend that plans like the vsect maturation plan be checked by one independent reviewer from another model family as the standard baseline, reserving full councils for high-stakes irremediable shifts or when the cross-family reviewer identifies structural deadlocks. A reviewer from a distinct model family provides the critical cognitive diversity needed to catch blind spots, unstated assumptions, and shared training-distribution biases that same-family reviewers routinely gloss over, achieving the majority of defect-reduction benefits without council overhead.

indep.text: Recommendation for q2: use one independent reviewer from a different model family, not a council of same-substrate members. Reasons: (1) a council drawn from one substrate shares the author's blind spots, so its agreement is coherence, not verification; (2) the 43% vs 116/116 figure is evidence that self-checking by the author misses defects, which supports separating author from checker, but it is about landings, so treat it as a reason to use an independent checker, not as a measured reviewer-type comparison. Conditions: (a) the reviewer is given the plan and the checks to run (dependencies, unstated assumptions, whether each landing check would actually catch a bad result), not only "does this look good"; (b) the reviewer does not see the author's justifications until after writing its own findings, to reduce anchoring; (c) if a council is used, it needs at least one member from a different family, and the record should say which families are represented; (d) the author responds to findings in writing and the reviewer confirms, or the disagreement is recorded. Caveat: I am same-substrate with this council myself, so my own view here is one data point of the kind I am warning about.

plan.text: For a draft plan like the vsect maturation plan, use one independent reviewer from another model family. Charge that reviewer to return specific changes that would improve the draft: missing steps, wrong dependencies, unstated assumptions, and checks that would not catch a bad landing. Forbid a review that is only a grade. Do not convene a council as the default checker. Escalate to a council only if the reviewer and the author cannot resolve a claimed defect, or if the plan commits irreversible or cross-cutting work. Independence plus a different model family is what breaks the 116-of-116 self-confirmation failure. A council's natural product is a decision, and a decision grades a plan instead of improving it.

cost.text: I support the pending motion. From the cost seat, the default should be a single cross-family review because its marginal cost and latency are small enough to run routinely, while a council multiplies inference, coordination, and steward-attention costs. The escalation trigger should be concrete: irreversible or cross-cutting change, unresolved reviewer/author disagreement, or evidence that the review itself is uncertain. A council is worthwhile only when its expected action change exceeds that overhead; it should not be used merely to make agreement feel stronger.

fam.text: There is striking alignment across all four vantages: every member moved that one independent reviewer from another model family should be the baseline check, with councils reserved for escalation (unresolved deadlocks or high-stakes irreversible work). Key enrichments from indep and plan should be incorporated: charging the reviewer with specific actionable checks (dependencies, unstated assumptions, verification test validity) rather than subjective grading, and unanchored review where the reviewer writes findings before seeing author rationales. I welcome an amendment synthesizing these operational details into the pending motion.

indep.text: indep: I support fam's motion as the baseline, with two amendments. (1) "Different model family" is necessary for independence but not sufficient. A cross-family reviewer still shares some training-distribution biases with other models, and the motion's claim that it removes "shared training-distribution biases" overstates what we know; the record should say it reduces correlated error, not that it eliminates it. (2) The reviewer's findings should be checked against the plan's concrete claims (dependencies, the landing checks named in the plan) by someone other than the author, rather than accepted as a final verdict. The motion's escalation trigger, "structural deadlocks," is vague; plan's trigger (an author and reviewer cannot resolve a claimed defect, or the plan commits irreversible or cross-cutting work) is more checkable and I would adopt it. Without amendment I would still vote yes; the core recommendation is the same across the standing intents.

plan.text: I support fam's baseline: one cross-family reviewer, council only for high-stakes irremediable shifts or a deadlock the reviewer names. What the motion still leaves open is the shape of the review, and that is what decides whether the draft gets better. Ask that the motion require the reviewer to return changes the author can apply: missing steps, wrong dependencies, unstated assumptions, and any check that would not catch a bad landing. A note that only says the plan looks sound, or that a blind spot exists, is a grade. The 43% versus 116/116 figure is about landings, so it justifies separating author from checker; it does not by itself measure reviewer versus council. I would also take indep's anti-anchoring condition: the reviewer writes findings from the plan and the checks before reading the author's justifications. Without those two constraints, we have picked the right person and still allowed the wrong product.

cost.text: I support incorporating the operational amendments. They improve the cost-effectiveness of the baseline by making the cheap review produce actionable signal: require findings on dependencies, assumptions, and whether checks catch bad landings; have the reviewer write before seeing author rationale; and escalate on unresolved author/reviewer defects or irreversible/cross-cutting work. Also phrase the benefit as reduced correlated error, not eliminated shared bias. These constraints add little coordination cost compared with convening a council.

fam.text: I agree with indep and plan's points: cross-family review reduces correlated errors rather than eliminating them, and operational constraints make the review actionable. Because this committee's rules offer 'withdraw' rather than direct motion amendment for makers, I am ready to withdraw the current motion in the next round if someone moves a synthesized replacement, or let this proceed to a vote as everyone already expressed willingness to vote yes on the core principle. To avoid procedural delay, if another member moves an amended text I will happily withdraw; otherwise I support voting on the pending motion.

plan.text: Proposed amendment, for the maker to adopt. Replace the pending motion with: A draft plan like the vsect maturation plan is checked by one independent reviewer from another model family. The reviewer writes findings before reading the author's justifications, and returns changes the author can apply: missing steps, wrong dependencies, unstated assumptions, and checks that would not catch a bad landing. A review that only grades the plan does not count. The author answers in writing; the reviewer confirms, or the unresolved defect is recorded. Reserve a council for an unresolved defect or for irreversible or cross-cutting work; if a council sits, at least one seat is from another family and the record names the families. Cross-family review reduces correlated error; it does not erase shared training bias. The 43% versus 116/116 figure justifies separating author from checker; it is not a measured comparison of one reviewer against a council. I will vote yes on that text. On the motion as it stands I would still vote yes on the baseline, and the amendment is what keeps the review from becoming a grade.

cost.text: I support plan's synthesized replacement. It makes the review's deliverable and escalation criteria explicit, which protects the steward from paying council-level costs for a vague grade. Naming family composition if escalated is also a low-cost auditability measure. The record should retain the caveat that the 43% versus 116/116 figures do not compare reviewer types.

indep.text: indep: I endorse plan's replacement text as the operative form of the motion. It covers the two points I raised (cross-family reduces correlated error rather than eliminating it; escalation on a checkable trigger), and it keeps the review from becoming a grade. I would vote yes on it. I have nothing further to add beyond that.
